en: Alas, my uncle, sultan and lion!
May our father be your sacrifice,
O luckless hero dearer than a father,
Without a word you made me cry out,
Why did you make me lament so?
Our sheep shared the same fold,
Our food the same fellowship,
Whatever we found, we gathered together,
We shared death and shared the faith.
Our grazing herds and encampment were one,
Our lives and our common death were one.
When we entered battle, we shared its dust,
Our lives and destined death were one,
Though I pleaded and stared imploringly,
You stared in confusion like a mute.
His bearing was proud, his eyes deep black,
Tall in stature and broad of shoulder,
Both strongman and lionhearted hero,
A luckless hero capable of making
The whole world submit.
He looked from side to side,
Licking his lips,
Roaring in anger,
Shouting fearsomely.
His redness was like dun-colored fur,
And if you heard his cry,
It was like a lion's roar.
His eyes were like embers of saxaul,
When his gray mane crackled,
It was like a bolt of lightning,
Such was the sight of his power.
His giant frame was like a lion,
No soul could withstand his terror,
But panicked, unable to find a way out.
He seemed to swoop upon whomever he met,
And bear them off like a giant bird,
Fearing nothing beneath the moon and sky;
Allah Most High indeed creates
His servants in every form,
And such was Külchoro's form.
The space between his shoulders
Was like a field sown with grain;
Would anyone who challenged
That wrathful gray-maned hero remain alive?
The corners of his eyes were like flint,
As though this gray-maned hero could swallow the world
At the mere sound of his name.
If you looked at his ears,
The poor man bore the mark of a fortress,
As though he sucked out men's souls in combat.
His wildness was like a boar's,
His crackling like dry straw,
And a rash enemy who fought him
Could neither measure nor master his strength.
His charge was like a whirlwind.
I am dead, not alive,
Yet instead of dying I became an ember,
Living on as I waited for you.
Appearing alive, you made me rejoice,
Only to burn and scorch me utterly.
Vanishing beyond sight,
You abandoned livestock and household without a guardian.
When I catch hold of you, you say nothing;
Why did you begin acting like a helpless wretch?
For pity's sake, uncle, speak—
What my eyes saw from the ridge!
Would it not have been far better
Had you died instead of living?
Exalting your lionhearted pride,
You conceal your words without speaking,
You have knocked the wind from me,
You have quenched and chilled my breath.
Tell me your words, uncle;
If you stand there suddenly
Without speaking or uttering a sound,
And my wrath rises till I stand rigid,
A mighty quarrel will suddenly erupt.
The mystic's cave will turn to dust,
The face of the earth will run red with blood.
If I roar out in anger,
Those I encounter will lie dead,
So take care, lest I spring suddenly.
I may pounce upon you without warning!”
So spoke Külchoro,
His lionlike nature showing,
His furious rage pouring out.
His beard was like a quiver case,
His upright mustache
Like the haft of a greasy axe;
Such was Choro when you saw him.
He looked every bit the hero one could desire;
When wrath made him stand rigid,
He seemed ready to devour whoever challenged him,
Such was Külchoro's nature.
Broad-chested, with a spacious breast,
Such was Külchoro's nature,
His bloodlust seized him.
Power surged from his imposing frame,
And from the fire of his two cheeks
Sprang enough hair to fill a stocking.
Whenever Külchoro grew impassioned,
He would take his spear in his right hand,
And when wrath made him stand rigid,
He would bring slaughter upon the world.
When he truly gripped its shaft,
When the lone champion took it in hand,
He would scout the road alone,
Rout Jeti-Kait and seize its spoils.
If an enemy boasted of strength,
He shook down the mightiest.
He drove strongmen into flight,
And when an enemy came to grapple,
He drove his black-steel spear
Deep between his ribs.
When Semetey's cause fell to him,
Elkindi became his mountain encampment.
He made the whole world submit,
A lionhearted hero who spared himself nothing.
He flashed like a bird of prey,
Cracked like a white musket,
And spoke without holding back.
The tiger he held did not move
Or stir in the slightest.
He thundered in fury,
As though about to deal death,
As though about to take the bloodthirsty hero's life,
As though about to cut off his head,
Carry it to his son Seytek and Chürök,
And plunge the gray-maned hero into turmoil,
Then take the severed head
To Khan Bakai and Kanykei,
To those two aged ones,
And announce the glad news.
His forearms were thick as a strongman's,
As though he might bring slaughter upon the world.
If anyone challenged his wrath,
He seemed ready to swallow whoever crossed him.
Such was Choro when you saw him,
A lionhearted hero supported by the spirits,
Renowned as a hero and ruler of the people,
A steel fortress in Talas for Kyrgyz and Argyn,
Through which no wind could pass.
Since this bloodthirsty hero slipped from his grasp,
His anguish had been immense,
His burning grief a fire of hell,
His wandering a black and lightless night,
Until he burned, died down, and became ash.
While the valiant gray-maned hero lived,
He exulted above all other mortals.
When the valiant hero passed from sight,
He withered under boundless torment.
The deeply grieving Külchoro
Was struck by dawn upon the road.
Good heavens, when the valiant man fell into his hands—
He spoke no word and uttered no sound,
There was no eye that had truly seen him,
No word that he had returned alive;
If said to be dead, he was not in the grave,
If said to be alive, he was nowhere among men,
If said to be safe, he was not among the herds.
His insides ached and his breast was aflame,
And he had no kinsman besides Choro.
What exists today is gone tomorrow;
Such filth, it seems, is this world.
Then Külchoro
Began pouring out his words,
And if the gray-maned lion would not heed
The words he poured forth, he would kill him.
Choking with resentment,
His temper darkly changed,
He ground his teeth until they cracked,
His eyes blazing with rage,
As though he would camp along the Seven Valleys,
As though he would swallow the whole world,
His lion's eyes blazed,
I have poured away much of my strength,
I have made a stake of my arm,
I have spilled my blood by the spoonful.
To this blackhearted bloodthirsty man
I shall now sacrifice
My precious life, no greater than a fly.
I shall ask his inmost secret,
And if he will not tell it,
My wrath shall rise till I stand rigid,
And I shall do something to this bloodthirsty man.
Why should I go on living as a slave;
What else remains for me to do?”
So saying, Külchoro
Drew a line as a sign;
The poor falcon among men
Was about to do something extraordinary.
He was about to begin disaster,
About to inflame the madness,
That incurable, festering wound.
He was about to bring upon the hero
A calamity no man had ever seen.
Refusing to release the young man,
He was about to tear his mind apart.
Standing rigid in his rage,
He held fast to his lord,
The dear one who had made him helpless.
How could he ever release
That man whose stature loomed like a mountain?
Allah Most High indeed creates
His servants in every form.
Some souls He made heroes,
Some He made lionhearted warriors,
Some souls He made deficient,
And some souls the Creator made
Equal to the dark grave.
Then Külchoro,
Clashing and refusing to let go,
Clung to the bloodthirsty lion.
He began circling through his speech,
Hurling out forceful words,
Each word's ending
Devouring anyone who understood.
Heedless of your vastness,
Showing mercy to no living soul,
Heedless of the blessed lion,
The poor hero who had endured many ordeals
Did not spare his threadlike life.
“Why does he stand there without speaking?
Why does God strike
This witless, bloodthirsty sultan?” he said.
“For this I have been diminished,
Yet he gives no thought to me;
For this I was taken into slavery,
Yet he does not grieve for me at all.
I spent my precious youth,
And made a club of my head.”
When Külchoro and Kara Döö together seized Semetey, saying, “Now that I have caught you,
I shall not leave you alive but kill you,” Külchoro grew angry and said, “Neither entering
The grave in death nor living among your people, you made me bear your torment. Now,
If I do not kill you and then die myself, unless you renounce the life of this world, speak
A word to me, or come to your senses”—and in his fury Külchoro seized his lord,
Shaking him and refusing to let go. Then Semetey, frightened by Külchoro's voice,
Began to speak:
He seized him and twisted his mouth,
Standing rigid in his rage,
And spoke to him harshly.
As he spoke so harshly,
At that moment Semetey
Quietly began speaking weighty words:
“It is indeed true that you were parted
And left without the one dear to you.
You were a man whose glory loomed like a mountain,
And it is also true that, parted from your noble one,
You were left humiliated.
The sable cap upon one's head—
Who would not wear it at a jaunty tilt?
While fortune rests upon one's head,
Who would not stride about thundering?
You were parted and separated,
Enduring shame and grieving.
What you have said is indeed true;
